claim: Translation initiation of most eukaryotic mRNAs depends on recruitment of methionyl initiator tRNA (Met-tRNAi) in a ternary complex (TC) with GTP-bound eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) to the small (40S) ribosomal subunit.
source: Initiating translation of most eukaryotic mRNAs depends on recruitment of methionyl initiator tRNA (Met-tRNAi) in a ternary complex (TC) with GTP-bound eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) to the small (40S) ribosomal subunit, forming a 43S preinitiation complex (PIC) that attaches to the mRNA and scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′ UTR) for an AUG start codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical translation initiation mechanism in eukaryotes.

claim: The 43S preinitiation complex attaches to the mRNA and scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′ UTR) for an AUG start codon.
source: Initiating translation of most eukaryotic mRNAs depends on recruitment of methionyl initiator tRNA (Met-tRNAi) in a ternary complex (TC) with GTP-bound eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) to the small (40S) ribosomal subunit, forming a 43S preinitiation complex (PIC) that attaches to the mRNA and scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′ UTR) for an AUG start codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the scanning mechanism of translation initiation.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A has been implicated in GTP-independent binding of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit and its recruitment to specialized mRNAs that do not require scanning.
source: Previous studies have implicated mammalian eIF2A in GTP-independent binding of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit and its recruitment to specialized mRNAs that do not require scanning, and in initiation at non-AUG start codons, when eIF2 function is attenuated by phosphorylation of its α-subunit during stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on mammalian eIF2A.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A has been implicated in initiation at non-AUG start codons when eIF2 function is attenuated by phosphorylation of its α-subunit during stress.
source: Previous studies have implicated mammalian eIF2A in GTP-independent binding of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit and its recruitment to specialized mRNAs that do not require scanning, and in initiation at non-AUG start codons, when eIF2 function is attenuated by phosphorylation of its α-subunit during stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on mammalian eIF2A function under stress conditions.

claim: The eIF2AΔ mutation conferred no significant TE reductions for any mRNAs in non-starved cells.
source: Whereas starvation of WT confers changes in translational efficiencies (TEs) of hundreds of mRNAs, the eIF2AΔ mutation conferred no significant TE reductions for any mRNAs in non-starved cells, and it reduced the TEs of only a small number of transcripts in starved cells containing phosphorylated eIF2α.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The eIF2AΔ mutation reduced the TEs of only a small number of transcripts in starved cells containing phosphorylated eIF2α.
source: Whereas starvation of WT confers changes in translational efficiencies (TEs) of hundreds of mRNAs, the eIF2AΔ mutation conferred no significant TE reductions for any mRNAs in non-starved cells, and it reduced the TEs of only a small number of transcripts in starved cells containing phosphorylated eIF2α.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eliminating eIF2A did not alter the translation of mRNAs containing putative internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements in non-starved or starved cells.
source: We found no evidence that eliminating eIF2A altered the translation of mRNAs containing putative internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements, or harboring uORFs initiated by AUG or near-cognate start codons, in non-starved or starved cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eliminating eIF2A did not alter the translation of mRNAs harboring uORFs initiated by AUG or near-cognate start codons in non-starved or starved cells.
source: We found no evidence that eliminating eIF2A altered the translation of mRNAs containing putative internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements, or harboring uORFs initiated by AUG or near-cognate start codons, in non-starved or starved cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Very few mRNAs (possibly only one) appear to employ eIF2A for Met-tRNAi recruitment in yeast cells, even when eIF2 function is attenuated by stress.
source: Thus, very few mRNAs (possibly only one) appear to employ eIF2A for Met-tRNAi recruitment in yeast cells, even when eIF2 function is attenuated by stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comprehensive ribosome profiling and validation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 43S PIC attaches to the 5′-end of the mRNA, activated by eIF4F bound to the m7G cap.
source: The 43S PIC attaches to the 5′-end of the mRNA, activated by eIF4F bound to the m7G cap (comprised of cap-binding protein eIF4E, scaffolding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A) and scans the 5′ UTR to identify the AUG start codon, using complementarity with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi to recognize the AUG triplet.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the scanning mechanism of translation initiation.

claim: eIF4F is comprised of cap-binding protein eIF4E, scaffolding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A.
source: The 43S PIC attaches to the 5′-end of the mRNA, activated by eIF4F bound to the m7G cap (comprised of cap-binding protein eIF4E, scaffolding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A) and scans the 5′ UTR to identify the AUG start codon, using complementarity with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi to recognize the AUG triplet.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the eIF4F complex.

claim: The 43S PIC scans the 5′ UTR to identify the AUG start codon using complementarity with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi to recognize the AUG triplet.
source: The 43S PIC attaches to the 5′-end of the mRNA, activated by eIF4F bound to the m7G cap (comprised of cap-binding protein eIF4E, scaffolding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A) and scans the 5′ UTR to identify the AUG start codon, using complementarity with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi to recognize the AUG triplet.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of start codon recognition.

claim: The 48S PIC arrested at the start codon joins with the large (60S) subunit to form an 80S initiation complex ready to synthesize the first peptide bond in protein synthesis.
source: The 48S PIC arrested at the start codon joins with the large (60S) subunit to form an 80S initiation complex ready to synthesize the first peptide bond in protein synthesis (reviewed in Hinnebusch, 2014; Shirokikh and Preiss, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the final steps of translation initiation, supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of the α-subunit of eIF2 converts eIF2-GDP from substrate to inhibitor of its guanine nucleotide exchange factor, eIF2B, diminishing TC assembly.
source: A key mechanism for downregulating bulk translation initiation during stress entails phosphorylation of the α-subunit of eIF2, which converts eIF2-GDP from substrate to inhibitor of its guanine nucleotide exchange factor, eIF2B, diminishing TC assembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of translational control during stress.

claim: Translation of specialized mRNAs encoding certain stress-activated transcription factors regulated by inhibitory upstream open-reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs is induced rather than inhibited by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Translation of specialized mRNAs encoding certain stress-activated transcription factors regulated by inhibitory upstream open-reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs is induced rather than inhibited by eIF2α phosphorylation because the reduction in TC levels allows scanning PICs to bypass the uORF start codons and initiate further downstream at the start codon for the transcription factor coding sequences (CDS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about translational control of stress-response genes.

claim: The reduction in TC levels allows scanning PICs to bypass the uORF start codons and initiate further downstream at the start codon for the transcription factor coding sequences (CDS).
source: Translation of specialized mRNAs encoding certain stress-activated transcription factors regulated by inhibitory upstream open-reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs is induced rather than inhibited by eIF2α phosphorylation because the reduction in TC levels allows scanning PICs to bypass the uORF start codons and initiate further downstream at the start codon for the transcription factor coding sequences (CDS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of uORF-mediated translational control.

claim: The Integrated Stress Response in mammals governs the translational induction of GCN4 mRNA in budding yeast in response to amino acid starvation.
source: This mechanism, dubbed the Integrated Stress Response in mammals, governs the translational induction of GCN4 mRNA in budding yeast in response to amino acid starvation, dependent on the sole yeast eIF2α kinase, Gcn2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Integrated Stress Response, supported by citations.

claim: Translational induction of GCN4 mRNA in budding yeast in response to amino acid starvation is dependent on the sole yeast eIF2α kinase, Gcn2.
source: This mechanism, dubbed the Integrated Stress Response in mammals, governs the translational induction of GCN4 mRNA in budding yeast in response to amino acid starvation, dependent on the sole yeast eIF2α kinase, Gcn2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of Gcn2 in the stress response.

claim: The Gcn4 protein activates the transcription of multiple genes encoding amino acid biosynthetic enzymes.
source: The Gcn4 protein thus induced activates the transcription of multiple genes encoding amino acid biosynthetic enzymes (reviewed in Hinnebusch, 2005; Gunišová et al., 2018; Dever et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Gcn4, supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A has been implicated in translation initiation under stress conditions where eIF2 function is reduced by phosphorylation.
source: Various studies using cultured mammalian cells have implicated the auxiliary initiation factor eIF2A in translation initiation under stress conditions where eIF2 function is reduced by phosphorylation, in non-canonical initiation events where an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) bypasses the scanning mechanism for selecting AUG codons, or when a near-cognate codon (NCC) rather than AUG serves as initiation site (reviewed in Komar and Merrick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on mammalian eIF2A, as indicated by the citation.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A has been implicated in non-canonical initiation events where an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) bypasses the scanning mechanism for selecting AUG codons.
source: Various studies using cultured mammalian cells have implicated the auxiliary initiation factor eIF2A in translation initiation under stress conditions where eIF2 function is reduced by phosphorylation, in non-canonical initiation events where an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) bypasses the scanning mechanism for selecting AUG codons, or when a near-cognate codon (NCC) rather than AUG serves as initiation site (reviewed in Komar and Merrick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on mammalian eIF2A, as indicated by the citation.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A has been implicated in initiation when a near-cognate codon (NCC) rather than AUG serves as initiation site.
source: Various studies using cultured mammalian cells have implicated the auxiliary initiation factor eIF2A in translation initiation under stress conditions where eIF2 function is reduced by phosphorylation, in non-canonical initiation events where an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) bypasses the scanning mechanism for selecting AUG codons, or when a near-cognate codon (NCC) rather than AUG serves as initiation site (reviewed in Komar and Merrick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on mammalian eIF2A, as indicated by the citation.

claim: eIF2A was originally characterized as a factor purified from rabbit reticulocytes that could stimulate GTP-independent recruitment of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit in response to an AUG codon.
source: eIF2A was originally characterized as a factor purified from rabbit reticulocytes that could stimulate GTP-independent recruitment of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit in response to an AUG codon, but could not stimulate the same reaction on native globin mRNA (Adams et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adams et al., 1975.

claim: eIF2A could not stimulate GTP-independent recruitment of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit on native globin mRNA.
source: eIF2A was originally characterized as a factor purified from rabbit reticulocytes that could stimulate GTP-independent recruitment of Met-tRNAi to the 40S subunit in response to an AUG codon, but could not stimulate the same reaction on native globin mRNA (Adams et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adams et al., 1975.

claim: The stimulation of Met-tRNAi binding by eIF2A was actually conferred by a protein co-purifying with eIF2A, identified as ligatin/eIF2D.
source: Later studies suggested that the stimulation of Met-tRNAi binding was actually conferred by a protein co-purifying with eIF2A, identified as ligatin/eIF2D (Dmitriev et al., 2010; Skabkin et al., 2010), which was subsequently implicated in ribosome recycling at termination codons (reviewed in Dever and Green, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dmitriev et al., 2010 and Skabkin et al., 2010.

claim: Ligatin/eIF2D was subsequently implicated in ribosome recycling at termination codons.
source: Later studies suggested that the stimulation of Met-tRNAi binding was actually conferred by a protein co-purifying with eIF2A, identified as ligatin/eIF2D (Dmitriev et al., 2010; Skabkin et al., 2010), which was subsequently implicated in ribosome recycling at termination codons (reviewed in Dever and Green, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dever and Green, 2012.

claim: eIF2A could functionally substitute for eIF2 in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the AUG start codons of Sindbis virus 26S mRNA when eIF2α is phosphorylated in virus-infected cells.
source: Experiments in cultured cells suggested that eIF2A could functionally substitute for eIF2 in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the AUG start codons of viral mRNAs, including Sindbis virus 26S mRNA (Ventoso et al., 2006) and HCV mRNA (Kim et al., 2011), which is driven by an IRES, when eIF2α is phosphorylated in the virus-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ventoso et al., 2006 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: eIF2A could functionally substitute for eIF2 in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the AUG start codons of HCV mRNA, which is driven by an IRES, when eIF2α is phosphorylated in virus-infected cells.
source: Experiments in cultured cells suggested that eIF2A could functionally substitute for eIF2 in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the AUG start codons of viral mRNAs, including Sindbis virus 26S mRNA (Ventoso et al., 2006) and HCV mRNA (Kim et al., 2011), which is driven by an IRES, when eIF2α is phosphorylated in the virus-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ventoso et al., 2006 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: eIF2A functionally cooperates with eIF5B in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the 40S-HCV IRES PIC.
source: Other evidence suggested that eIF2A functionally cooperates with eIF5B in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the 40S-HCV IRES PIC (Kim et al., 2018), and it was implicated in IRES-dependent translation of c-SRC mRNA (Kwon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2018.

claim: eIF2A was implicated in IRES-dependent translation of c-SRC mRNA.
source: Other evidence suggested that eIF2A functionally cooperates with eIF5B in recruiting Met-tRNAi to the 40S-HCV IRES PIC (Kim et al., 2018), and it was implicated in IRES-dependent translation of c-SRC mRNA (Kwon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kwon et al., 2017.

claim: Several independent studies did not support a role for eIF2A in initiation on Sindbis or HCV mRNAs.
source: However, several independent studies did not support a role for eIF2A in initiation on Sindbis or HCV mRNAs (Jaafar et al., 2016; Sanz et al., 2017; González-Almela et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jaafar et al., 2016; Sanz et al., 2017; González-Almela et al., 2018.

claim: Mammalian eIF2A was implicated in initiation at CUG initiation codons decoded by a leucyl-tRNA versus Met-tRNAi in producing polypeptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules.
source: Other lines of evidence implicated mammalian eIF2A in initiation at CUG initiation codons decoded by a leucyl-tRNA versus Met-tRNAi in producing polypeptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules (Starck et al., 2012); and in initiation at an upstream CUG codon to produce an N-terminally extended form of PTENα (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Starck et al., 2012.

claim: eIF2A was implicated in initiation at an upstream CUG codon to produce an N-terminally extended form of PTENα.
source: Other lines of evidence implicated mammalian eIF2A in initiation at CUG initiation codons decoded by a leucyl-tRNA versus Met-tRNAi in producing polypeptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules (Starck et al., 2012); and in initiation at an upstream CUG codon to produce an N-terminally extended form of PTENα (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2014.

claim: eIF2A was reported to support non-AUG initiation events involved in translation through an expansion of GGGGGC repeats present in the C9ORF72 gene in neuronal cells exhibiting elevated eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: eIF2A was also reported to support non-AUG initiation events involved in translation through an expansion of GGGGGC repeats present in the C9ORF72 gene in neuronal cells exhibiting elevated eIF2α phosphorylation (Sonobe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sonobe et al., 2018.

claim: eIF2A mediates initiation at UUG- or CUG-initiated uORFs in the 5′ UTR of BiP mRNA that appear to enhance BiP translation when eIF2α phosphorylation is induced by ER stress.
source: There is additional evidence that eIF2A mediates initiation at UUG- or CUG-initiated uORFs in the 5′ UTR of BiP mRNA that appear to enhance BiP translation when eIF2α phosphorylation is induced by ER stress (Starck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Starck et al., 2016.

claim: eIF2A has been implicated in stimulating translation of positive-acting uORFs initiated by CUG or other NCCs during tumor initiation in a manner important for tumor formation in animals.
source: eIF2A has also been implicated in stimulating translation of positive-acting uORFs initiated by CUG or other NCCs during tumor initiation in a manner important for tumor formation in animals (Sendoel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sendoel et al., 2017.

claim: eIF2A knock-out mice were found to exhibit reduced longevity, dysregulated lipid metabolism, obesity, decreased glucose tolerance, and increased insulin resistance—all phenotypes of metabolic syndrome.
source: Recently, eIF2A knock-out mice were found to exhibit reduced longevity, dysregulated lipid metabolism, obesity, decreased glucose tolerance, and increased insulin resistance—all phenotypes of metabolic syndrome—and also decreased lymphocyte production and compromised immune tolerance, implicating eIF2A in several important physiological processes and disease states.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of findings from eIF2A knock-out mice studies.

claim: eIF2A knock-out mice exhibited decreased lymphocyte production and compromised immune tolerance.
source: Recently, eIF2A knock-out mice were found to exhibit reduced longevity, dysregulated lipid metabolism, obesity, decreased glucose tolerance, and increased insulin resistance—all phenotypes of metabolic syndrome—and also decreased lymphocyte production and compromised immune tolerance, implicating eIF2A in several important physiological processes and disease states.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of findings from eIF2A knock-out mice studies.

claim: Mice lacking eIF2A did not exhibit defects in expression of BiP or CHOP upregulated by eIF2α phosphorylation during ER stress.
source: The mice lacking eIF2A, however, did not exhibit defects in expression of BiP or a protein (CHOP) upregulated by eIF2α phosphorylation during ER stress (Anderson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2021.

claim: The amino acid sequence of eIF2A is fairly well conserved between yeast and mammals across the length of the protein.
source: The amino acid sequence of eIF2A is fairly well conserved between yeast and mammals across the length of the protein (Komar and Merrick, 2020), raising the possibility that it might function in IRES-mediated translation or non-canonical initiation at NCC codons in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Komar and Merrick, 2020.

claim: Analysis of a yeast mutant lacking the gene encoding eIF2A (YGR054W) indicated that eIF2A did not participate in canonical, cap-dependent translation initiation, having no impact on bulk translation initiation in vivo.
source: Analysis of a yeast mutant lacking the gene encoding eIF2A (YGR054W) indicated, as might be expected, that eIF2A did not participate in canonical, cap-dependent translation initiation, having no impact on bulk translation initiation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies on yeast eIF2A.

claim: Yeast eIF2A was found to co-fractionate with 40S and 80S ribosomes.
source: Yeast eIF2A was found, however, to co-fractionate with 40S and 80S ribosomes and to interact genetically with canonical initiation factors eIF4E and eIF5B (Zoll et al., 2002; Komar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zoll et al., 2002 and Komar et al., 2005.

claim: Yeast eIF2A was found to interact genetically with canonical initiation factors eIF4E and eIF5B.
source: Yeast eIF2A was found, however, to co-fractionate with 40S and 80S ribosomes and to interact genetically with canonical initiation factors eIF4E and eIF5B (Zoll et al., 2002; Komar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zoll et al., 2002 and Komar et al., 2005.

claim: Analysis of the eIF2AΔ deletion mutant indicated that eIF2A functions to suppress, rather than enhance, non-canonical initiation events that occur independently of scanning.
source: Surprisingly, analysis of the deletion mutant (referred to below as eIF2AΔ) indicated that eIF2A functions to suppress, rather than enhance, non-canonical initiation events that occur independently of scanning, including an IRES identified in the URE2 mRNA (Komar et al., 2003; Komar et al., 2005; Reineke and Merrick, 2009; reviewed in Komar and Merrick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komar et al., 2003; Komar et al., 2005; Reineke and Merrick, 2009.

claim: eIF2A functions to suppress non-canonical initiation events including an IRES identified in the URE2 mRNA.
source: Surprisingly, analysis of the deletion mutant (referred to below as eIF2AΔ) indicated that eIF2A functions to suppress, rather than enhance, non-canonical initiation events that occur independently of scanning, including an IRES identified in the URE2 mRNA (Komar et al., 2003; Komar et al., 2005; Reineke and Merrick, 2009; reviewed in Komar and Merrick, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komar et al., 2003; Komar et al., 2005; Reineke and Merrick, 2009.

claim: The eIF2AΔ mutation did not alter expression of a reporter for the GCN4 transcript.
source: One piece of evidence arguing against this idea is that the eIF2AΔ mutation did not alter expression of a reporter for the GCN4 transcript (Zoll et al., 2002) that, as mentioned above, is induced by eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zoll et al., 2002.

claim: SM treatment of WT evoked a small reduction in the ratio of polysomes to monosomes (P/M), indicating a diminished rate of bulk translation initiation.
source: As we reported previously (Gaikwad et al., 2021), SM treatment of WT evoked a small reduction in the ratio of polysomes to monosomes (P/M), indicating a diminished rate of bulk translation initiation (Figure 1A(i) and (iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Gaikwad et al., 2021.

claim: Essentially identical P/M ratios were observed in the corresponding untreated and SM-treated eIF2AΔ mutant compared to WT.
source: Essentially identical P/M ratios were observed in the corresponding untreated and SM-treated eIF2AΔ mutant (Figure 1A(ii) and (iv)), suggesting that eIF2A does not function broadly to compensate for reduced eIF2 function in the yeast translatome.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: eIF2A does not function broadly to compensate for reduced eIF2 function in the yeast translatome.
source: Essentially identical P/M ratios were observed in the corresponding untreated and SM-treated eIF2AΔ mutant (Figure 1A(ii) and (iv)), suggesting that eIF2A does not function broadly to compensate for reduced eIF2 function in the yeast translatome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of identical P/M ratios in WT and eIF2AΔ mutant.

claim: The RPF and RNA read counts between biological replicates for each strain and condition were highly reproducible (Pearson's r ≈ 0.99).
source: The RPF and RNA read counts between biological replicates for each strain and condition were highly reproducible (Pearson's r ≈ 0.99) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–H.

claim: SM treatment induced comparable levels of eIF2α phosphorylation in both the WT and eIF2AΔ mutant.
source: To establish that SM treatment induced comparable levels of eIF2α phosphorylation in both the WT and eIF2AΔ mutant, we examined the ribosome profiling data for GCN4 mRNA, whose translation is induced by phosphorylated eIF2α by the specialized 'delayed reinitiation' mechanism imposed by the four uORFs in its transcript.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of GCN4 mRNA translation data.

claim: Translation of GCN4 uORF1 and uORF2 gives rise to 40S subunits that escape recycling at these uORF stop codons and resume scanning downstream.
source: Translation of the 5′-proximal uORFs (uORF1 and uORF2) gives rise to 40S subunits that escape recycling at these uORF stop codons and resume scanning downstream.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GCN4 translational control mechanism.

claim: At high TC levels, 40S subunits scanning downstream from GCN4 uORFs 1-2 quickly rebind TC and reinitiate at uORFs 3 or 4 and are efficiently recycled from the mRNA following their translation.
source: At high TC levels, they quickly rebind TC and reinitiate at uORFs 3 or 4 and are efficiently recycled from the mRNA following their translation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GCN4 translational control mechanism.

claim: When TC levels are reduced by eIF2α phosphorylation, a fraction of scanning 40S subunits fails to rebind TC until after bypassing uORFs 3–4, and then rebind the TC in time to reinitiate at the GCN4 CDS, inducing GCN4 translation.
source: When TC levels are reduced by eIF2α phosphorylation, a fraction of scanning 40S subunits fails to rebind TC until after bypassing uORFs 3–4, and then rebind the TC in time to reinitiate at the GCN4 CDS, inducing GCN4 translation (Figure 1B; reviewed in Hinnebusch, 2005; Gunišová et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GCN4 translational control mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Ribosome profiling revealed a strong induction of GCN4 translation evoked by SM treatment of WT cells, with an increase in TE (ΔTE) of ~40-fold.
source: Ribosome profiling revealed the expected strong induction of GCN4 translation evoked by SM treatment of WT cells, as revealed by greatly increased RPFs in the CDS with little or no change in GCN4 mRNA reads, yielding an increase in TE (ΔTE) of ~40-fold (Figure 1C, WT+SM versus WT, cf. replicate cultures _a and _b for RPFs and RNA reads).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Highly similar results for GCN4 translation induction were observed in the eIF2AΔ mutant in the presence and absence of SM.
source: Highly similar results were observed in the eIF2AΔ mutant in the presence and absence of SM (Figure 1C, eIF2AΔ+SM versus eIF2AΔ), indicating that eIF2α phosphorylation was induced by SM at comparable levels in both the mutant and WT strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: eIF2A does not contribute to recruitment of Met-tRNAi as an alternative to the TC by 40S subunits scanning downstream from GCN4 uORFs 1–2.
source: These data argue against the possibility that eIF2A contributes to recruitment of Met-tRNAi as an alternative to the TC by 40S subunits scanning downstream from GCN4 uORFs 1–2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GCN4 translation induction is similar in WT and eIF2AΔ mutant.

claim: DESeq2 analysis of the ribosome profiling data obtained for the eIF2AΔ mutant and WT strains cultured in the absence of SM revealed no significant TE reductions in the mutant, as no mRNAs exhibited TEeIF2AΔ/TEWT ratios < 1 at FDR < 0.25.
source: Importantly, DESeq2 analysis of the ribosome profiling data obtained for the eIF2AΔ mutant and WT strains cultured in the absence of SM revealed no significant TE reductions in the mutant, as no mRNAs exhibited TEeIF2AΔ/TEWT ratios < 1 at a false discovery rate (FDR < 0.25) that is appropriate for two highly correlated biological replicates (Lamarre et al., 2018; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Lamarre et al., 2018.

claim: Few, if any, mRNAs are appreciably dependent on eIF2A for translation initiation in nutrient-replete cells where TC is abundant.
source: This finding suggests that few, if any, mRNAs are appreciably dependent on eIF2A for translation initiation in nutrient-replete cells where TC is abundant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the DESeq2 analysis showing no significant TE reductions in eIF2AΔ mutant.

claim: SM treatment of WT cells leads to a broad reprogramming of translational efficiencies as DESeq2 analysis revealed hundreds of mRNAs exhibiting increases or decreases in relative TE even at the highly stringent FDR of < 0.01.
source: In addition to induction of GCN4 translation, SM treatment of WT cells leads to a broad reprogramming of translational efficiencies as DESeq2 analysis revealed hundreds of mRNAs exhibiting increases or decreases in relative TE even at the highly stringent FDR of < 0.01 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mRNAs that are efficiently translated in untreated WT cells tend to exhibit increased relative TEs when phosphorylation of eIF2α is induced by SM, whereas poorly translated mRNAs tend to show reduced relative TEs.
source: Previously, we presented evidence that many of these TE changes conform to a pattern in which mRNAs that are efficiently translated in untreated WT cells tend to exhibit increased relative TEs, whereas poorly translated mRNAs tend to show reduced relative TEs, when phosphorylation of eIF2α is induced by SM.
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: The same pattern of TE changes was evident under two other conditions in which 43S PIC assembly is reduced: impaired recycling of 40S subunits from post-termination complexes at stop codons and depletion of an essential 40S ribosomal protein.
source: This same pattern was evident under two other conditions in which 43S PIC assembly is reduced, impaired recycling of 40S subunits from post-termination complexes at stop codons and depletion of an essential 40S ribosomal protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: The stereotypical reprogramming of translation arises from increased competition among mRNAs for limiting PICs wherein strongly translated mRNAs outcompete weakly translated mRNAs to skew TE increases towards 'strong' mRNAs.
source: We proposed that this stereotypical reprogramming of translation arises from increased competition among mRNAs for limiting PICs wherein strongly translated mRNAs outcompete weakly translated mRNAs to skew TE increases towards 'strong' mRNAs (Gaikwad et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their previous work, as indicated by the citation.

claim: SM treatment of the eIF2AΔ mutant produced a broad reprogramming of TEs involving hundreds of mRNAs translated relatively better or worse on SM treatment.
source: SM treatment of the eIF2AΔ mutant also produced a broad reprogramming of TEs involving hundreds of mRNAs translated relatively better or worse on SM treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of transcripts showed TE changes in the same direction on SM treatment of WT and eIF2AΔ cells.
source: Comparing the TE changes conferred by SM in WT versus eIF2AΔ cells for the mRNAs showing TE changes in WT revealed that the majority of transcripts showed TE changes in the same direction on SM treatment of WT and eIF2AΔ cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A very strong positive correlation exists, with a coefficient of 0.91, between the TE changes conferred by SM in WT and eIF2AΔ strains.
source: Indeed, the majority of mRNAs dysregulated in the eIF2AΔ mutant also showed TE changes in the WT strain (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and a very strong positive correlation exists, with a coefficient of 0.91, between the TE changes conferred by SM in the two strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Elimination of eIF2A did not substantially alter the global reprogramming of translation produced by phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: Thus, elimination of eIF2A did not substantially alter the global reprogramming of translation produced by phosphorylation of eIF2α.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the strong correlation between TE changes in WT and eIF2AΔ strains upon SM treatment.

claim: The large group of 879 mRNAs that showed TE reductions on SM treatment of WT cells show a relatively smaller, not larger, decrease in median TE on SM treatment of the eIF2AΔ mutant versus SM treatment of WT.
source: Interrogating the large group of 879 mRNAs that showed TE reductions on SM treatment of WT cells revealed that they show a relatively smaller, not larger, decrease in median TE on SM treatment of the eIF2AΔ mutant versus SM treatment of WT (Figure 2D, column 12 versus column 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most mRNAs that showed TE reductions on SM treatment of WT cells exhibit a small increase in TE on comparing SM-treated eIF2AΔ to SM-treated WT cells.
source: Consistent with this finding, most of these mRNAs exhibit a small increase in TE on comparing SM-treated eIF2AΔ to SM-treated WT cells (Figure 2D, column 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of mRNAs whose translation is diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation in WT cells do not utilize eIF2A for a back-up initiation mechanism that would mitigate their TE reductions when eIF2 is impaired.
source: These results suggest that the majority of mRNAs whose translation is diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation in WT cells do not utilize eIF2A for a back-up initiation mechanism that would mitigate their TE reductions when eIF2 is impaired.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mRNAs with TE reductions in SM-treated WT do not show greater reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ.

claim: eIF2A generally acts to repress the translation of mRNAs whose translation is diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation rather than augmenting eIF2 function in Met-tRNAi recruitment when both WT and eIF2AΔ are treated with SM.
source: Our finding that most mRNAs exhibit somewhat greater TEs in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells when both are treated with SM (Figure 2D, column 11) might indicate that eIF2A generally acts to repress the translation of these mRNAs rather than augmenting eIF2 function in Met-tRNAi recruitment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A group of only 32 mRNAs showed significant TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells (TEeIF2AΔ+SM/TEWT+SM < 1, FDR < 0.25).
source: To determine whether there are any individual mRNAs that show greater TE reductions in response to SM treatment when eIF2A is absent, we conducted DESeq2 analysis of the TE changes in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells. A group of only 32 mRNAs showed significant TE reductions in this comparison, that is, TEeIF2AΔ+SM/TEWT+SM < 1, FDR < 0.25 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 32 mRNAs showing TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells showed nearly two-fold greater TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells compared to all mRNAs.
source: The TE reductions for this group of transcripts (designated ΔTEeIF2AΔ+SM/WT+SM_down) in comparison to all mRNAs were nearly two-fold greater in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells (Figure 3B, column 1), which are the results expected if they utilize eIF2A as a back-up when eIF2 is impaired by phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 32 mRNAs showing TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells also showed TE reductions in SM-treated versus untreated eIF2AΔ cells, albeit of lesser magnitude.
source: They also showed TE reductions in SM-treated versus untreated eIF2AΔ cells, albeit of lesser magnitude (Figure 3B, column 2), also in the manner expected if eIF2 and eIF2A play redundant roles in their translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Functional redundancy between eIF2 and eIF2A is supported by the findings that both SM treatment of WT cells and elimination of eIF2A from untreated cells does not reduce the median TEs of the 32 mRNAs showing TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells.
source: Functional redundancy is further supported by the findings that both SM treatment of WT cells and elimination of eIF2A from untreated cells does not reduce their median TEs (Figure 3B, columns 3–4), as only one of the two factors is impaired or eliminated in these latter comparisons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The median TE of the 32 mRNAs showing TE reductions in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells increases rather than decreases on SM treatment of WT.
source: The fact that the median TE of these mRNAs increases rather than decreases on SM treatment of WT (Figure 3B, column 3) might be explained by proposing that their ability to rely on eIF2A provides them with a competitive advantage with mRNAs that depend solely on eIF2 when the latter is impaired by phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only 17 of the 32 transcripts displayed the diagnostic pattern of an appreciable reduction in TE both on elimination of eIF2A in SM-treated cells and on SM treatment of cells lacking eIF2A but either a lesser reduction, no change, or increase in TE on SM treatment of WT cells and on elimination of eIF2A from untreated cells.
source: Only 17 of the 32 transcripts (marked with '#') displayed the diagnostic pattern of an appreciable reduction in TE both on elimination of eIF2A in SM-treated cells and on SM treatment of cells lacking eIF2A (red or pink hues in columns 1–2 of Figure 3C), but either a lesser reduction, no change, or increase in TE on SM treatment of WT cells and on elimination of eIF2A from untreated cells (light pink, white or blue hues in columns 3–4 of Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only the HKR1 reporter displayed a significantly greater reduction in expression in response to SM treatment in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells among the 12 LUC reporters tested.
source: Assaying these LUC reporters in both WT and eIF2AΔ cells in the presence and absence of SM showed that only the HKR1 reporter displayed a significantly greater reduction in expression in response to SM treatment in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Except for HKR1 mRNA, the LUC reporter analysis failed to support a conditional requirement for eIF2A for the candidate genes examined.
source: Hence, except for HKR1 mRNA, the LUC reporter analysis failed to support a conditional requirement for eIF2A for the candidate genes examined.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results.

claim: Only three transcripts, HKR1, SAG1, and SVL3, displayed a greater TE reduction in response to SM treatment of eIF2AΔ cells compared to SM treatment of WT by polysome profiling analysis.
source: Analyzing the results from three biological replicates for WT versus eIF2AΔ cells ± SM revealed that only three transcripts, HKR1, SAG1, and SVL3, displayed a greater TE reduction in response to SM treatment of eIF2AΔ cells compared to SM treatment of WT (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the HKR1 transcript satisfied all of the criteria for conditional eIF2A dependence in ribosome profiling data in a manner confirmed by both reporter analysis and polysome profiling.
source: Thus, only the HKR1 transcript satisfied all of the criteria for conditional eIF2A dependence in ribosome profiling data in a manner confirmed by both reporter analysis and polysome profiling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of ribosome profiling, reporter analysis, and polysome profiling.

claim: There are very few mRNAs, possibly only one, that utilize eIF2A as a back-up for eIF2 in recruitment of tRNAi when eIF2 is impaired by phosphorylation.
source: We conclude that there are very few mRNAs, possibly only one, that utilize eIF2A as a back-up for eIF2 in recruitment of tRNAi when eIF2 is impaired by phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of ribosome profiling, reporter assays, and polysome profiling.

claim: No significant change in TE or ribosome occupancy for URE2 mRNA was found on deletion of eIF2A in either non-starved or SM-starved cells.
source: We next interrogated our ribosome profiling data for the effects of deleting eIF2A on translation of URE2 mRNA, reported to contain an IRES that is inhibited by eIF2A (Komar et al., 2005). We found no significant change in TE or ribosome occupancy for URE2 mRNA on deletion of eIF2A in either non-starved or SM-starved cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4A and a citation to Komar et al., 2005.

claim: No significant alteration in TEs of GIC1 and PAB1 mRNAs was found between eIF2AΔ and WT cells in the presence or absence of SM treatment.
source: It was reported that yeast mRNAs GIC1 and PAB1 also contain IRESs and are subject to translational repression by eIF2A (Reineke and Merrick, 2009); however, we again found no significant alteration in their TEs between eIF2AΔ and WT cells in the presence or absence of SM treatment (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4B and C and a citation to Reineke and Merrick, 2009.

claim: The results do not support a role for eIF2A in repressing IRES function in yeast cells.
source: Our results do not support a role for eIF2A in repressing IRES function in yeast cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling data for URE2, GIC1, and PAB1 mRNAs.

claim: CPA1 mRNA encodes an arginine biosynthetic enzyme and contains a single AUG-initiated inhibitory uORF that attenuates translation of the main CDS in cells replete with arginine.
source: In addition to GCN4 described above, CPA1 mRNA, encoding an arginine biosynthetic enzyme, contains a single AUG-initiated inhibitory uORF that attenuates translation of the main CDS in cells replete with arginine (Werner et al., 1987; Delbecq et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Werner et al., 1987 and Delbecq et al., 1994.

claim: An approximately two-fold increase in the TE of CPA1 mRNA was observed on SM treatment of WT cells.
source: In accordance with previous findings that the inhibitory effects of single uORFs can be diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation by allowing scanning ribosomes to bypass the uORF start codon (Young and Wek, 2016; Dever et al., 2023), we observed an approximately two-fold increase in the TE of CPA1 mRNA on SM treatment of WT cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Young and Wek, 2016 and Dever et al., 2023.

claim: The TE change of CPA1 mRNA conferred by SM treatment was not significantly altered by the eIF2AΔ mutation.
source: However, this TE change was not significantly altered by the eIF2AΔ mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data for CPA1 mRNA.

claim: YAP2/CAD1 mRNA contains two inhibitory AUG uORFs.
source: Similarly, for the well-characterized YAP2/CAD1 mRNA, containing two inhibitory AUG uORFs (Vilela et al., 1998), we observed a 2.6-fold TE increase conferred by SM in WT cells that, again, was not significantly altered by deletion of eIF2A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vilela et al., 1998.

claim: A 2.6-fold TE increase of YAP2/CAD1 mRNA was observed conferred by SM in WT cells.
source: Similarly, for the well-characterized YAP2/CAD1 mRNA, containing two inhibitory AUG uORFs (Vilela et al., 1998), we observed a 2.6-fold TE increase conferred by SM in WT cells that, again, was not significantly altered by deletion of eIF2A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The TE increase of YAP2/CAD1 mRNA conferred by SM was not significantly altered by deletion of eIF2A.
source: Similarly, for the well-characterized YAP2/CAD1 mRNA, containing two inhibitory AUG uORFs (Vilela et al., 1998), we observed a 2.6-fold TE increase conferred by SM in WT cells that, again, was not significantly altered by deletion of eIF2A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The eIF2AΔ deletion had no effect on the TEs of CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 in non-starved cells.
source: The eIF2AΔ deletion also had no effect on the TEs of CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 in non-starved cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data for CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs.

claim: Translational repression exerted by the uORFs in CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs is mitigated by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Thus, although we found evidence that translational repression exerted by the uORFs in CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs is mitigated by eIF2α phosphorylation, it appears that eIF2A has little or no role in recognizing the AUG codons of these uORFs in the presence or absence of diminished TC levels, just as we concluded above for the GCN4 uORFs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling data for CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs.

claim: eIF2A has little or no role in recognizing the AUG codons of the uORFs in CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs in the presence or absence of diminished TC levels.
source: Thus, although we found evidence that translational repression exerted by the uORFs in CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs is mitigated by eIF2α phosphorylation, it appears that eIF2A has little or no role in recognizing the AUG codons of these uORFs in the presence or absence of diminished TC levels, just as we concluded above for the GCN4 uORFs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling data for CPA1 and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs.

claim: A group of 1306 mRNAs containing 2720 uORFs, initiating with either AUG or one of the nine NCCs, showed evidence of translation in multiple ribosome profiling datasets from various mutant and WT strains.
source: Looking more broadly, we interrogated a previously identified group of 1306 mRNAs containing 2720 uORFs, initiating with either AUG or one of the nine NCCs, that showed evidence of translation in multiple ribosome profiling datasets from various mutant and WT strains (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: A set of 791 mRNAs containing 982 AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs are both evolutionarily conserved and show evidence of translation in ribosome profiling experiments.
source: We also analyzed a second set of 791 mRNAs containing 982 AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs that are both evolutionarily conserved and show evidence of translation in ribosome profiling experiments (Spealman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spealman et al., 2018.

claim: Four groups of mRNAs with translated AUG- or NCC-uORFs showed little or no TE change for their CDSs on SM treatment of WT cells.
source: These four groups of mRNAs with translated AUG- or NCC-uORFs showed little or no TE change for their CDSs on SM treatment of WT cells (Figure 6A(i)–(ii), columns 4 and 7 versus 1), indicating that, in contrast to GCN4, CPA1, and YAP2/CAD1 mRNAs, most of them do not contain inhibitory uORFs that can be bypassed in response to eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both groups of mRNAs containing either AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs exhibit very small, albeit highly significant, reductions in CDS TEs in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells in the absence of SM.
source: Both groups of mRNAs containing either AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs exhibit very small, albeit highly significant, reductions in CDS TEs in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells in the absence of SM (Figure 6A(i)–(ii), columns 5 and 8 versus 2); however, the same was not observed for the effects of eIF2AΔ in SM-treated cells where eIF2 function is attenuated (Figure 6(i)–(ii), columns 6 and 9 versus 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Groups of 557 mRNAs containing AUG-initiated uORFs and 191 mRNAs with NCC-uORFs were identified in which the uORFs were shown to influence translation of downstream CDSs by massively parallel analysis of reporters.
source: Recently, groups of 557 mRNAs containing AUG-initiated uORFs and 191 mRNAs with NCC-uORFs were identified in which the uORFs were shown to influence translation of downstream CDSs by massively parallel analysis of reporters containing the native 5′ UTRs in comparison to mutant reporters lacking the uORF start codons (May et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to May et al., 2023.

claim: Among the 407 mRNAs containing a single functional AUG-uORF wherein mutating the uORF significantly altered reporter expression by >1.5-fold, all but 13 of the uORFs functioned to inhibit reporter expression.
source: It was reported that among the 407 mRNAs containing a single functional AUG-uORF wherein mutating the uORF significantly altered reporter expression by >1.5-fold, all but 13 of the uORFs functioned to inhibit reporter expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to a previous report.

claim: Among the 144 mRNAs containing a single functional NCC-uORF, only 13 of the uORFs influenced reporter expression either positively or negatively by >1.5-fold.
source: Among the 144 mRNAs containing a single functional NCC-uORF, only 13 of the uORFs influenced reporter expression either positively or negatively by >1.5-fold, reflecting the weaker effects of NCC- versus AUG-initiated uORFs on downstream translation (May et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to May et al., 2023.

claim: Analysis of the 394 mRNAs containing a single inhibitory AUG-uORF revealed little or no change in median TE in response to SM treatment or to the eIF2AΔ mutation in the presence or absence of SM.
source: Our analysis of the 394 mRNAs containing a single inhibitory AUG-uORF—the only group large enough for statistical analysis of TE changes—revealed little or no change in median TE in response to SM treatment or to the eIF2AΔ mutation in the presence or absence of SM (Figure 6A(iii), columns, 4–6 versus 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: eIF2A has a minimal role in determining whether functional inhibitory AUG-initiated uORFs are translated or bypassed by scanning ribosomes in the presence or absence of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: These findings suggest that eIF2A has a minimal role in determining whether functional inhibitory AUG-initiated uORFs are translated or bypassed by scanning ribosomes in the presence or absence of eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of mRNAs containing single inhibitory AUG-uORFs.

claim: The majority of mRNAs containing translated uORFs show little response to either eIF2α phosphorylation, the elimination of eIF2A, or a combination of both perturbations.
source: These results support our findings above that the majority of mRNAs containing translated uORFs show little response to either eIF2α phosphorylation, the elimination of eIF2A, or a combination of both perturbations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of uORF-containing mRNAs.

claim: Subsets of uORF-containing mRNAs that exhibit >1.41-fold increases in TE in response to SM treatment of WT cells are novel candidates for mRNAs controlled by inhibitory uORFs that can be overcome by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: We probed more deeply into the three sets of uORF-containing mRNAs mentioned above by examining the subsets of each group that exhibit >1.41-fold increases in TE in response to SM treatment of WT cells, making them novel candidates for mRNAs controlled by inhibitory uORFs that can be overcome by eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of uORF-containing mRNAs showing TE increases upon SM treatment.

claim: These uORF-containing mRNAs showing appreciable TE increases upon SM treatment exhibit median TE increases of approximately two-fold on SM treatment of WT cells.
source: These uORF-containing mRNAs exhibit median TE increases of approximately two-fold on SM treatment of WT cells (Figure 6B(i)–(iii), maroon data), similar to the findings above for CPA1 and CAD1 mRNAs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Subsets of uORF-containing mRNAs showing appreciable TE induction by SM exhibit slightly reduced median TEs in response to the eIF2AΔ mutation in SM-treated, but not untreated cells.
source: Unlike the larger groups of uORF-containing mRNAs from which they derive (analyzed in Figure 6A(i)–(iii)), these subsets showing appreciable TE induction by SM exhibit slightly reduced median TEs in response to the eIF2AΔ mutation in SM-treated, but not untreated cells (Figure 6B(i)–(iii), green versus orange data).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: These mRNAs generally contain a positive-acting uORF that functions to overcome the translational barrier imposed by a second inhibitory uORF located further downstream in response to eIF2α phosphorylation, accounting for their increased TE conferred by SM treatment of WT cells.
source: One way to explain these findings would be to hypothesize that these mRNAs generally contain a positive-acting uORF that functions to overcome the translational barrier imposed by a second inhibitory uORF located further downstream in response to eIF2α phosphorylation, in the manner established for the positive-acting uORF1 in GCN4 mRNA, accounting for their increased TE conferred by SM treatment of WT cells.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the observed TE changes.

claim: The TE reductions conferred by eIF2AΔ exclusively in SM-treated cells would arise from loss of eIF2A-dependent translation of the stimulatory upstream uORFs in these transcripts required for scanning ribosomes to bypass the downstream inhibitory uORFs when eIF2α is phosphorylated.
source: The TE reductions conferred by eIF2AΔ exclusively in SM-treated cells would then arise from loss of eIF2A-dependent translation of the stimulatory upstream uORFs in these transcripts required for scanning ribosomes to bypass the downstream inhibitory uORFs when eIF2α is phosphorylated.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the observed TE changes.

claim: All three groups of mRNAs (containing annotated or conserved AUG-uORFs, annotated or conserved NCC-uORFs, or functional inhibitory AUG-uORFs) showing >1.41-fold reduction in TE in SM-treated eIF2AΔ versus SM-treated WT cells show TE reductions in response to the eIF2AΔ mutation only in the presence of SM.
source: Examining all such mRNAs containing either (i) annotated or conserved AUG-uORFs (Figure 6C(i)), (ii) annotated or conserved NCC-uORFs (Figure 6(ii)), or (iii) functional inhibitory AUG-uORFs (Figure 6C(iii)) revealed that all three groups show TE reductions in response to the eIF2AΔ mutation only in the presence of SM (green versus orange data) and, except for the NCC-uORF mRNAs, also show TE increases in response to SM in WT cells (Figure 6C(i)–(iii), maroon data), generally supporting the aforementioned hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Of the 17 mRNAs showing highly significant TE reductions conferred by eIF2AΔ in SM-treated cells versus SM treatment of WT, only 3 (YFL027C, YKL082C, and YLR330W/CHS5) contain a functional AUG- or NCC-initiated uORF.
source: Of these 17 mRNAs, only 3 (YFL027C, YKL082C, and YLR330W/CHS5) contain a functional AUG- or NCC-initiated uORF (Figure 6D), which does not represent a statistically significant enrichment for such mRNAs (p = 0.21).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LUC reporter and polysome profiling analyses of YLR330W/CHS5 failed to confirm a conditional dependence for eIF2A.
source: Moreover, our LUC reporter and polysome profiling analyses of one of these three transcripts, YLR330W/CHS5, failed to confirm a conditional dependence for eIF2A (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The one mRNA for which conditional eIF2A dependence was confirmed, YDR420W/HKR1, does not contain a functional or conserved uORF nor even one merely showing evidence of translation in ribosome profiling experiments.
source: The one mRNA for which conditional eIF2A dependence was confirmed, YDR420W/HKR1, does not contain a functional or conserved uORF nor even one merely showing evidence of translation in ribosome profiling experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of HKR1 mRNA in the context of uORF-containing mRNAs.

claim: There is no compelling evidence that conditional dependence on eIF2A for efficient translation in SM-treated cells is conferred by positive-acting regulatory uORFs.
source: Thus, we could not find compelling evidence that conditional dependence on eIF2A for efficient translation in SM-treated cells is conferred by positive-acting regulatory uORFs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of uORF-containing mRNAs.

claim: No mRNAs exhibited significant changes in RRO in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT in the absence or presence SM, even at a relatively non-stringent FDR of 0.5.
source: We found that no mRNAs exhibited significant changes in RRO in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT in the absence or presence SM, even at a relatively non-stringent FDR of 0.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The groups of mRNAs with annotated or conserved AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs showed little or no difference in median RRO in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells in the absence or presence of SM.
source: Furthermore, the groups of mRNAs with annotated or conserved AUG- or NCC-initiated uORFs showed little or no difference in median RRO in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells in the absence or presence of SM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H, yellow versus blue data).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: The median RRO values are generally higher for mRNAs containing AUG-initiated versus NCC-initiated uORFs in the presence or absence of SM.
source: At least for the annotated uORFs, the median RRO values are generally higher for mRNAs containing AUG-initiated versus NCC-initiated uORFs in the presence or absence of SM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and G, blue data), as would be expected from more efficient initiation at AUG versus NCC start codons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and G.

claim: The results provide no compelling evidence that eIF2A frequently enhances initiation at negative-acting uORFs initiated by either AUG or NCC start codons in either starved or non-starved cells.
source: Thus, our results provide no compelling evidence that eIF2A frequently enhances initiation at negative-acting uORFs initiated by either AUG or NCC start codons in either starved or non-starved cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RRO analysis of uORF-containing mRNAs.

claim: Translation elongation factor eIF5A acts broadly to stimulate the rates of decoding and termination, but is particularly important for certain combinations of codons, which include stretches of proline codons and various three-codon combinations of Proline (Pro), aspartic acid (Asp), and glyine (Gly) codons.
source: Translation elongation factor eIF5A acts broadly to stimulate the rates of decoding and termination, but is particularly important for certain combinations of codons, which include stretches of proline codons and various three-codon combinations of Proline (Pro), aspartic acid (Asp), and glyine (Gly) codons (Saini et al., 2009; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Schuller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saini et al., 2009; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Schuller et al., 2017.

claim: Slower decoding rates for certain codon combinations were detected by ribosome profiling of yeast cells depleted of eIF5A by computing pause scores for all ~8000 three-amino acid motifs.
source: Slower decoding rates for these codon combinations were detected by ribosome profiling of yeast cells depleted of eIF5A by computing pause scores for all ~8000 three-amino acid motifs (Schuller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuller et al., 2017.

claim: Analyzing ribosome profiling data revealed no significant increase in pause scores for any tripeptide motif in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells.
source: Analyzing our profiling data revealed no significant increase in pause scores for any tripeptide motif in the eIF2AΔ mutant versus WT cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A marked increase in pause scores for all tripeptide motifs with valine (Val) in the third position was observed in WT cells treated with SM versus untreated WT cells.
source: As a positive control for the analysis, we examined our data on WT cells treated or untreated with SM, observing a marked increase in pause scores for all tripeptide motifs with valine (Val) in the third position, placing the corresponding Val codons in the A-site of the decoding ribosomes (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Increased pausing at tripeptide motifs with Val in the third position is expected from reduced levels of charged valyl-tRNA on inhibition of valine biosynthesis by SM and attendant slower decoding of all Val codons.
source: Increased pausing at these motifs is expected from reduced levels of charged valyl-tRNA on inhibition of valine biosynthesis by SM and attendant slower decoding of all Val codons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known mechanism of SM action and the observed pause score increases.

claim: eIF2A plays no major role in stimulating translation elongation through particular tripeptide motifs.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that eIF2A plays no major role in stimulating translation elongation through particular tripeptide motifs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pause score analysis.

claim: A synthetic growth phenotype was observed on combining the eIF2AΔ mutation with a temperature-sensitive mutation affecting eIF4E.
source: As noted above, a synthetic growth phenotype was observed on combining the eIF2AΔ mutation with either a temperature-sensitive mutation affecting eIF4E (Komar et al., 2005) or deletion of the FUN12 gene encoding eIF5B (Zoll et al., 2002), suggesting functional interactions between eIF2A and these initiation factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komar et al., 2005 and Zoll et al., 2002.

claim: A synthetic growth phenotype was observed on combining the eIF2AΔ mutation with deletion of the FUN12 gene encoding eIF5B.
source: As noted above, a synthetic growth phenotype was observed on combining the eIF2AΔ mutation with either a temperature-sensitive mutation affecting eIF4E (Komar et al., 2005) or deletion of the FUN12 gene encoding eIF5B (Zoll et al., 2002), suggesting functional interactions between eIF2A and these initiation factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komar et al., 2005 and Zoll et al., 2002.

claim: The profile of genetic interactions observed for the eIF2AΔ mutation was found to significantly resemble that of an ade1Δ mutation.
source: The profile of genetic interactions observed for the eIF2AΔ mutation was found to significantly resemble that of an ade1Δ mutation, including synthetic growth defects in eIF2AΔ double mutants containing deletions of genes HPT1 and FCY2, whose products function in purine base and cytosine uptake (Fcy2) or in synthesizing purine nucleotides from purine bases via the salvage pathway (Hpt1) (Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to a global analysis of synthetic phenotypes and a citation to Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012.

claim: Synthetic growth defects were observed in eIF2AΔ double mutants containing deletions of genes HPT1 and FCY2.
source: The profile of genetic interactions observed for the eIF2AΔ mutation was found to significantly resemble that of an ade1Δ mutation, including synthetic growth defects in eIF2AΔ double mutants containing deletions of genes HPT1 and FCY2, whose products function in purine base and cytosine uptake (Fcy2) or in synthesizing purine nucleotides from purine bases via the salvage pathway (Hpt1) (Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to a global analysis of synthetic phenotypes and a citation to Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012.

claim: Fcy2 functions in purine base and cytosine uptake.
source: The profile of genetic interactions observed for the eIF2AΔ mutation was found to significantly resemble that of an ade1Δ mutation, including synthetic growth defects in eIF2AΔ double mutants containing deletions of genes HPT1 and FCY2, whose products function in purine base and cytosine uptake (Fcy2) or in synthesizing purine nucleotides from purine bases via the salvage pathway (Hpt1) (Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012.

claim: Hpt1 functions in synthesizing purine nucleotides from purine bases via the salvage pathway.
source: The profile of genetic interactions observed for the eIF2AΔ mutation was found to significantly resemble that of an ade1Δ mutation, including synthetic growth defects in eIF2AΔ double mutants containing deletions of genes HPT1 and FCY2, whose products function in purine base and cytosine uptake (Fcy2) or in synthesizing purine nucleotides from purine bases via the salvage pathway (Hpt1) (Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012.

claim: No reduction in growth was detected in the fcy2ΔeIF2AΔ double mutant versus either single mutant or the WT strain in the presence or absence of adenine supplements.
source: To test this possibility, we generated the fcy2ΔeIF2AΔ double mutant and tested it for growth on synthetic minimal (SD) or synthetic complete (SC) medium supplemented with varying concentrations of adenine. Contrary to expectations, we failed to detect any reduction in growth in the double mutant versus either single mutant or the WT strain in the presence or absence of adenine supplements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The eIF2AΔ mutation conferred no significant reductions in the RPFs, mRNA levels, or TEs of any of 17 genes involved in de novo purine biosynthesis in non-starvation conditions.
source: We also interrogated our ribosome profiling data to examine the effects of the eIF2AΔ mutation on expression of the 17 yeast genes encoding proteins involved in de novo synthesis of inosine, adenine, or guanine nucleotides (Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012). The eIF2AΔ mutation conferred no significant reductions in the RPFs, mRNA levels, or TEs of any of 17 genes in non-starvation conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data and a citation to Ljungdahl and Daignan-Fornier, 2012.

claim: Assaying lacZ reporters for IMD2 and IMD3 in cells cultured under the conditions of ribosome profiling experiments revealed no significant reductions in expression conferred by elimination of eIF2A.
source: Moreover, assaying lacZ reporters for two such genes, IMD2 and IMD3, in cells cultured under the conditions of our ribosome profiling experiments revealed no significant reductions in expression conferred by elimination of eIF2A (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The findings do not support the possibility that eIF2A promotes expression of the biosynthetic genes for de novo purine biosynthesis.
source: Our findings do not support the possibility that eIF2A promotes expression of the biosynthetic genes for de novo purine biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling and reporter assay data for purine biosynthesis genes.

claim: At an SM concentration adequate to reduce bulk polysome assembly and strongly derepress translation of GCN4 mRNA in WT cells, neither response was detectably altered by the eIF2AΔ mutation.
source: At an SM concentration adequate to reduce bulk polysome assembly and strongly derepress translation of GCN4 mRNA in WT cells, neither response was detectably altered by the eIF2AΔ mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profiling and ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ribosome profiling revealed a broad reprogramming of translational efficiencies conferred by SM treatment of WT cells, which appeared to be essentially intact in cells lacking eIF2A.
source: Ribosome profiling revealed a broad reprogramming of translational efficiencies conferred by SM treatment of WT cells, noted previously (Gaikwad et al., 2021), wherein efficiently translated mRNAs tend to show increased relative TEs at the expense of poorly translated mRNAs, which also appeared to be essentially intact in cells lacking eIF2A.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data and a citation to Gaikwad et al., 2021.

claim: Only three mRNAs in the entire translatome were significantly altered in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells in the absence of SM, with all three showing higher, not lower, TEs in the mutant.
source: Interrogating the TE changes of individual mRNAs, we found only three in the entire translatome that were significantly altered in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells in the absence of SM, with all three showing higher, not lower, TEs in the mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: We failed to identify even a single mRNA among the 5340 transcripts with evidence of translation that is dependent on eIF2A for efficient translation in non-stressed cells containing normal levels of TC assembly.
source: Thus, we failed to identify even a single mRNA among the 5340 transcripts with evidence of translation that is dependent on eIF2A for efficient translation in non-stressed cells containing normal levels of TC assembly.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: Under conditions of SM treatment, 32 mRNAs showed significantly reduced TEs in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells, consistent with the possibility that they require eIF2A for Met-tRNAi recruitment only when TC assembly is diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Under conditions of SM treatment, we identified 32 mRNAs showing significantly reduced TEs in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells, consistent with the possibility that they require eIF2A for Met-tRNAi recruitment only when TC assembly is diminished by eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only 17 of the 32 transcripts showing reduced TEs in eIF2AΔ versus WT cells under SM treatment showed a pattern of TE changes fully consistent with a conditional requirement for eIF2A under conditions of reduced eIF2 function.
source: However, only 17 of these transcripts showed a pattern of TE changes fully consistent with a conditional requirement for eIF2A under conditions of reduced eIF2 function, exhibiting greater TE decreases when both eIF2 function was impaired by phosphorylation and eIF2A was eliminated from cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: We could validate conditional eIF2A dependence by LUC reporter analysis and by measuring TE changes of native mRNAs by polysome profiling for only a single mRNA, HKR1.
source: Moreover, we could validate this conditional eIF2A dependence by LUC reporter analysis and by measuring TE changes of native mRNAs by polysome profiling for only a single mRNA, HKR1.
evidence: This claim is supported by LUC reporter assay and polysome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings indicate a very limited role of yeast eIF2A in providing a back-up mechanism for Met-tRNAi recruitment when eIF2 function is diminished by phosphorylation of its α-subunit.
source: Given that native mRNAs were examined in the orthogonal assay of polysome profiling in Figure 3E, the positive results obtained there for SAG1 and SVL3 in addition to HKR1 should be given greater weight. Nevertheless, our findings indicate a very limited role of yeast eIF2A in providing a back-up mechanism for Met-tRNAi recruitment when eIF2 function is diminished by phosphorylation of its α-subunit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of ribosome profiling, reporter assays, and polysome profiling.

claim: Eliminating eIF2A had no effect on the TEs of CPA1 and CAD1 mRNAs, which contain single inhibitory uORFs that appear to be suppressed by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: We also looked intensively at groups of mRNAs containing uORFs to determine if eIF2A might promote uORF translation and thereby influence translation of the downstream CDSs. As observed for GCN4 mRNA, eliminating eIF2A had no effect on the TEs of CPA1 and CAD1 mRNAs, which contain single inhibitory uORFs that appear to be suppressed by eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data for CPA1 and CAD1 mRNAs.

claim: Little evidence was found for a significant role of eIF2A in either increasing or decreasing the TEs of mRNAs containing translated uORFs with AUG or NCC start codons.
source: We interrogated three different compilations of yeast mRNAs containing translated uORFs containing AUG or NCC start codons, including those with functional evidence of controlling translation of the downstream CDSs or showing evolutionary sequence conservation and, once again, found little evidence for a significant role of eIF2A in either increasing or decreasing the TEs of such transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by comprehensive analysis of uORF-containing mRNAs in ribosome profiling data.

claim: No evidence was found indicating that eIF2A inhibits utilization of IRES elements identified previously in URE2, PAB1, and GIC1 mRNAs.
source: We also found no evidence indicating that eIF2A inhibits utilization of IRES elements identified previously in URE2, PAB1, and GIC1 mRNAs; although, our results could be explained if the IRESs make only small contributions to the overall translation of these mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data for URE2, PAB1, and GIC1 mRNAs.

claim: No evidence was found that eIF2A affects the rate of decoding of any particular tripeptide motifs in the elongation phase of protein synthesis.
source: Finally, we found no evidence that eIF2A affects the rate of decoding of any particular tripeptide motifs in the elongation phase of protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by pause score analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: The lack of evidence for eIF2A function in translation initiation stands in contrast to findings of negative genetic interactions between the eIF2AΔ and mutations in yeast eIF4E and eIF5B.
